topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Acne Vulgaris & Breakouts (Pimples / Keel Muhase)
patient_answer: Wash your face twice daily with a gentle, non-comedogenic foaming cleanser and lukewarm water; do NOT scrub vigorously.
For mild acne: Over-the-counter topical Benzoyl Peroxide (2.5% to 5% gel) or Salicylic Acid wash kills acne bacteria and clears blocked pores.
For stubborn acne: Consult a dermatologist for topical retinoids (such as Adapalene 0.1% gel applied at bedtime in a pea-sized amount).
Always use an oil-free, non-comedogenic moisturizer and broad-spectrum sunscreen daily; acne treatments can cause mild peeling.
NEVER pop, squeeze, or pick at pimples; popping forces infection deeper into the skin and causes permanent pitted scarring and dark pigmentation.

doctor_answer.assessment: Acne Vulgaris (multifactorial follicular disease: follicular hyperkeratinization, Cutibacterium acnes colonization, excess sebum production, and inflammation). Classify severity: Mild (comedonal), Moderate (papulopustular), Severe (nodulocystic).
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. Endocrine evaluation (Total testosterone, DHEAS, LH/FSH) if adult female with hirsutism or irregular menses (rule out PCOS).
doctor_answer.management: Mild: Topical Retinoid (Adapalene 0.1%) + Topical Benzoyl Peroxide (BPO 2.5-5%). Moderate: Topical Retinoid + BPO + Topical/Oral Antibiotic (Doxycycline 100 mg daily for max 8-12 weeks; always combine with BPO to prevent resistance). Severe nodulocystic / scarring: Oral Isotretinoin (0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day; strict teratogenicity / pregnancy prevention protocol).
references: AAD Guidelines of Care for the Management of Acne Vulgaris
European Evidence-Based Guidelines for the Treatment of Acne

staff_answer: Verify patient does not squeeze pimples. Check pregnancy status before any oral retinoid prescription.
red_flags: Severe nodulocystic acne with scarring (requires oral Isotretinoin)
Sudden explosive severe acne with joint pain and fever (Acne Fulminans)
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: NEVER squeeze or pop pimples (causes permanent scarring)
NEVER take oral Isotretinoin during pregnancy (severe teratogenicity / birth defects)
source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) & European Dermatology Forum

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Fungal Skin Infections (Ringworm / Tinea / Daad)
patient_answer: Ringworm (Tinea) is a fungal infection of the skin that forms red, circular, raised, ring-shaped patches with clear centers and scaly, itchy borders.
Common locations: Body (Tinea corporis), Groin (Tinea cruris / Jock itch), and Feet (Tinea pedis / Athlete's foot).
Apply a topical antifungal cream (such as Clotrimazole 1%, Terbinafine 1%, or Luliconazole 1%) twice daily, covering 2 cm beyond the border of the rash.
Continue applying the cream for at least 1 to 2 weeks AFTER the rash completely disappears to eradicate deep fungal spores.
Keep the skin completely clean and dry; wear loose, breathable cotton clothing and change innerwear twice daily in humid weather.

STRICT DANGER WARNING: NEVER apply steroid creams (like Betnovate, Panderm, Quadriderm, Dermovate) to a fungal rash; steroids temporarily reduce itching but supercharge the fungal growth, causing extensive, treatment-resistant infection.

doctor_answer.assessment: Dermatophytosis (Tinea Corporis / Cruris / Pedis, caused by Trichophyton, Microsporum, or Epidermophyton genera). Recognize Tinea Incognito (fungal infection masked and exacerbated by improper topical corticosteroid abuse).
doctor_answer.investigations: KOH direct microscopic mount of skin scrapings (demonstrating septate branching hyphae). Fungal culture if refractory.
doctor_answer.management: Localized: Topical allylamine (Terbinafine 1% cream BID for 2-3 weeks) or topical azole (Luliconazole 1% or Sertaconazole). Extensive / recalcitrant / steroid-modified: Oral Antifungal (Oral Terbinafine 250 mg daily for 2-4 weeks or Itraconazole 100-200 mg daily for 2-4 weeks; monitor LFTs). STRICTLY PROHIBIT topical corticosteroids.
references: IADVL Guidelines for Management of Dermatophytosis in India
CDC Fungal Diseases: Ringworm Treatment

staff_answer: Ask explicitly if patient applied mixed steroid-antifungal-antibiotic creams (Panderm/Quadriderm). Prohibit steroids.
red_flags: Extensive body involvement covering > 30% body surface area (Steroid-modified Tinea Incognito)
Secondary bacterial cellulitis from deep scratching
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: STRICTLY AVOID applying topical steroid creams (Betnovate, Panderm, Quadriderm) to fungal infections
Do NOT share towels, bedsheets, or soap with family members
source: Indian Association of Dermatologists, Venereologists and Leprologists (IADVL) & CDC

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis) Care & Flare Control
patient_answer: Eczema is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by a damaged skin barrier leading to dry, intensely itchy, red, cracked patches (commonly in elbow and knee creases).

Moisturize, moisturize, moisturize: Apply a thick, fragrance-free emollient ointment or cream (petroleum jelly, ceramide cream) immediately within 3 minutes of stepping out of the shower while skin is still damp.
Take short baths (5 to 10 minutes) in lukewarm (never hot) water using mild, soap-free cleansers.
Wear smooth, 100% breathable cotton clothing; avoid scratchy wool, synthetic fabrics, and scented laundry detergents.
Keep fingernails trimmed short; scratching damages the skin barrier and introduces dangerous bacterial infections.
Consult a doctor during flare-ups for short courses of topical anti-inflammatory creams (mild corticosteroid or topical calcineurin inhibitor).

doctor_answer.assessment: Atopic Dermatitis (chronic relapsing pruritic inflammatory dermatosis associated with epidermal barrier dysfunction [filaggrin gene mutations] and immune dysregulation).
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical diagnosis (Hanifin and Rajka criteria). Skin swab culture only if secondary bacterial impetiginization.
doctor_answer.management: Stepped care: 1. Baseline: Liberal emollient therapy (>=250-500 g/week), avoidance of irritants. 2. Acute flares: Low-to-medium potency Topical Corticosteroids (Hydrocortisone 1% for face; Triamcinolone or Mometasone for body) applied BID for 5-14 days. 3. Maintenance: Proactive twice-weekly topical calcineurin inhibitor (Tacrolimus 0.03-0.1% ointment). Systemic biologics (Dupilumab) for severe refractory disease.
references: AAD Guidelines of Care for the Management of Atopic Dermatitis
NICE Guideline CG57: Atopic eczema in under 12s

staff_answer: Examine distribution (flexural creases in children/adults, cheeks/extensors in infants). Reinforce liberal emollient application.
red_flags: Rapid outbreak of painful, punched-out, umbilicated blisters with fever (Eczema Herpeticum - Medical Emergency requiring IV Acyclovir)
Honey-colored crusting indicating secondary Staphylococcal infection
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT take long, scalding hot baths (strips skin lipids and severely worsens itching)
Do NOT use fragranced soaps, bubble baths, or harsh perfumed detergents
source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) & NICE Guideline CG57

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Hives & Acute Urticaria (Allergic Wheals / Chhapaki)
patient_answer: Hives (Urticaria) are raised, red or pink, intensely itchy skin welts of varying shapes and sizes that appear suddenly and individual welts typically fade within 24 hours without leaving scars.
Common triggers: Viral infections (most common in children), food allergies, antibiotics or painkillers (NSAIDs), insect stings, or sudden temperature changes.
Take a modern, non-drowsy oral second-generation antihistamine (such as Cetirizine 10 mg, Fexofenadine 180 mg, or Bilastine 20 mg) for rapid relief of itching and wheals.
Apply soothing calamine lotion or cool damp cloths to relieve intense itching.
Take lukewarm baths; avoid hot water, tight belts, and strenuous exercise while hives are active.
EMERGENCY WARNING (ANAPHYLAXIS): Seek emergency care immediately if hives are accompanied by swelling of your lips, tongue, or eyelids, difficulty breathing, throat tightness, or dizziness.

doctor_answer.assessment: Acute Urticaria (< 6 weeks duration). Mast cell degranulation releasing histamine and inflammatory mediators. Must assess for systemic Anaphylaxis and Angioedema.
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. Allergy testing not indicated for self-limiting acute episodes unless clear anaphylaxis trigger.
doctor_answer.management: First-line: Second-generation non-sedating H1-antihistamines (Cetirizine 10 mg, Fexofenadine 180 mg, Bilastine 20 mg daily; dose can be titrated up to 4-fold under physician supervision for stubborn wheals). Short-course oral Prednisolone (20-30 mg daily for 3-5 days) reserved only for severe acute angioedema. Discontinue suspect culprit medications.
references: EAACI/GA²LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI Guideline for the Definition, Classification, Diagnosis, and Management of Urticaria
WAO Guidelines

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Red if facial/lip swelling, throat tightness, or dyspnea (Anaphylaxis); Green if isolated hives. Check airway and vitals.
red_flags: Swelling of lips, tongue, uvula, or difficulty swallowing (Angioedema)
Wheezing, stridor, or shortness of breath
Dizziness, fainting, or SBP < 90 mmHg (Anaphylactic Shock - STAT IM Epinephrine)
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT take Ibuprofen, Aspirin, or NSAIDs during an urticaria outbreak (frequently worsens hives dramatically)
Do NOT scratch vigorously
source: EAACI/GA²LEN/WAO Urticaria Guidelines & World Allergy Organization

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Scabies Mite Infestation (Nocturnal Itching)
patient_answer: Scabies is caused by microscopic mites (Sarcoptes scabiei) that burrow into the upper layer of the skin to live and lay eggs, triggering an intense allergic reaction.
Hallmark sign: Severe, unbearable itching that becomes DRAMATICALLY WORSE AT NIGHT in bed or after a hot bath.
Common locations: Tiny pimple-like bumps and thin wavy gray/red burrow lines between the fingers, wrists, armpits, waist, navel, and genital area.
TREATMENT PROCEDURE: Apply 5% Permethrin dermal cream over your entire body from the neck down to the tips of your toes, leaving it on for 8 to 14 hours (overnight) before washing off.
REPEAT APPLICATION: Apply the treatment again exactly 7 days later to eradicate any newly hatched mites.
ALL HOUSEHOLD CONTACTS MUST BE TREATED ON THE SAME NIGHT, even if they have zero itching, to prevent endless reinfection.
Wash all bedsheets, towels, and clothing in hot water (at least 50°C / 122°F) and dry on high heat.

doctor_answer.assessment: Scabies Infestation. Highly contagious ectoparasitosis. Differentiate classic scabies from Crusted (Norwegian) scabies in immunocompromised patients.
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. Dermoscopy ('delta-wing' jet sign), skin scraping with mineral oil microscopy (identifies mites, eggs, scybala).
doctor_answer.management: First-line: Topical Permethrin 5% cream applied neck-to-toes for 8-14 hours, repeated on Day 8. Oral Ivermectin (200 mcg/kg single dose with food, repeated on Day 8-14) for institutional outbreaks or topical failures. Mandatory simultaneous treatment of all household contacts. Oral antihistamines and topical hydrocortisone for post-scabetic pruritus (persists 2-4 weeks after mite death).
references: CDC Scabies Treatment Guidelines
IUSTI European Guideline for the Management of Scabies

staff_answer: Confirm that ALL household members are treated on the same night. Instruct hot water laundering of bedding.
red_flags: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies: thick warty hyperkeratotic crusts containing millions of mites (highly infectious, requires oral Ivermectin + topical Permethrin)
Secondary bacterial cellulitis
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT treat only one family member while ignoring household contacts (causes immediate reinfection loop)
Do NOT assume ongoing itch in the first 2 weeks means treatment failed (post-scabetic itch takes weeks to settle)
source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) & International Alliance for the Control of Scabies

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Psoriasis (Scaly Plaques & Flakes)
patient_answer: Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune condition that speeds up the lifecycle of skin cells, causing cells to build up rapidly on the surface into thick, silvery-scaled red plaques.
Common areas: Knees, elbows, scalp, lower back, and nails (nail pitting or discoloration).
Moisturize daily: Apply thick emollient ointments immediately after bathing to soften scales and soothe dryness.
Take short lukewarm baths with Epsom salts or oatmeal to gently loosen thick plaques; do NOT vigorously pick or scrape scales.
Sensible sunlight exposure (10-15 minutes of mild morning sun) can help slow skin cell proliferation.
Consult a dermatologist for specialized treatments: prescription Vitamin D analogues (Calcipotriol), topical corticosteroids, targeted phototherapy (narrowband UVB), or modern biologic therapies.

doctor_answer.assessment: Plaque Psoriasis (Psoriasis Vulgaris, T-cell mediated autoimmune dermatosis). Screen for Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA: DIP joint involvement, dactylitis 'sausage digit', enthesitis) and metabolic syndrome.
doctor_answer.investigations: Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI score). Screen for PsA using PEST questionnaire. Baseline LFT, lipid profile, fasting glucose, hepatitis/TB screen prior to systemic agents.
doctor_answer.management: Mild (<3-5% BSA): Topical Corticosteroid + Topical Vitamin D3 analogue (Calcipotriol/Betamethasone combination ointment). Moderate-to-Severe (>10% BSA or refractory): Narrowband UVB Phototherapy, Systemic non-biologics (Methotrexate 10-25 mg ONCE WEEKLY, Apremilast), or Biologic therapy (anti-TNF, anti-IL-17, anti-IL-23).
references: AAD-NPF Guidelines of Care for the Management and Treatment of Psoriasis
NICE Guideline CG153: Psoriasis: assessment and management

staff_answer: Inspect joints and nails (pitting, onycholysis). Screen for joint pain and dactylitis.
red_flags: Joint pain, morning stiffness, or swollen 'sausage' fingers/toes (Psoriatic Arthritis - requires urgent systemic therapy to prevent joint destruction)
Sudden generalized redness and skin shedding over >90% body (Erythrodermic Psoriasis - Medical Emergency)
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT aggressively pick, peel, or scratch scales (triggers the Koebner phenomenon, where injury creates new plaques)
Do NOT stop systemic psoriasis medications abruptly
source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) & National Psoriasis Foundation (NPF)

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Dandruff & Seborrheic Dermatitis (Scalp Flakes)
patient_answer: Dandruff is a mild form of seborrheic dermatitis driven by sensitivity to a naturally occurring harmless scalp yeast called Malassezia.
Key signs: Itchy scalp, white or yellowish greasy flakes in your hair and on your shoulders, and redness along the hairline, eyebrows, sides of the nose, and ears.
In infants: Known as 'Cradle Cap' (thick, yellowish, greasy crusts on the baby's scalp), which is harmless and usually resolves on its own.
Effective treatment for adults: Use an anti-dandruff shampoo containing Ketoconazole 2%, Zinc Pyrithione, Selenium Sulfide, or Salicylic Acid 2 to 3 times a week.
CRUCIAL SHAMPOO TECHNIQUE: Lather the shampoo into your scalp and LEAVE IT ON FOR 5 FULL MINUTES before rinsing out, allowing the active antifungal medicine time to work.
Avoid applying heavy hair oils (mustard oil, heavy coconut oil); excess oil feeds the Malassezia yeast and worsens inflammation.

doctor_answer.assessment: Seborrheic Dermatitis (inflammatory dermatosis involving sebum-rich areas, driven by Malassezia yeast colonization and altered sebum lipid profile). Differentiate from scalp psoriasis (thick silvery micaceous scales).
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. Rule out underlying HIV or Parkinson's disease if acute, severe, or generalized recalcitrant seborrheic dermatitis.
doctor_answer.management: Adult scalp: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo or Ciclopirox 1% shampoo twice weekly (leave on scalp for 5 minutes). Mild topical corticosteroid lotion or topical calcineurin inhibitor for facial/ear involvement. Infant cradle cap: Softening with mineral oil/coconut oil followed by gentle soft-brush combing and gentle baby shampoo.
references: AAD Guidelines on Seborrheic Dermatitis
British Association of Dermatologists Guidelines

staff_answer: Instruct patient on leaving antifungal shampoo on scalp for full 5 minutes before rinsing.
red_flags: Severe refractory seborrheic dermatitis in young adult (consider HIV testing)
Secondary bacterial infection with impetigo crusts
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT apply heavy cooking or hair oils to active seborrheic dermatitis (feeds the yeast)
Do NOT wash shampoo off instantly (requires 5-minute contact time)
source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) & British Association of Dermatologists

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Warts (Verrucae) & Molluscum Contagiosum
patient_answer: Common warts are benign skin growths caused by Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection of the outer skin layer, commonly appearing on fingers, hands, and feet (plantar warts).
Molluscum Contagiosum is another common viral skin infection (frequent in children) causing small, firm, dome-shaped, pearly bumps with a tiny dimple in the center.
Both are spread through direct skin-to-skin contact, sharing towels, or walking barefoot around damp swimming pool decks.

Home treatment for warts: Over-the-counter Salicylic acid liquid or wart pads: soak wart in warm water for 5 minutes, gently file dead skin with an emery board, apply medicine strictly to the wart, and cover with tape.
Never scratch, pick, or bite warts; scratching spreads the virus to surrounding skin.
Consult a dermatologist for stubborn warts: treatments include cryotherapy (freezing with liquid nitrogen), chemical peeling, or laser removal.

doctor_answer.assessment: Verruca Vulgaris / Plantar Warts (HPV types 1, 2, 4, 27, 57) and Molluscum Contagiosum (Poxvirus). Benign epidermal proliferations with high rates of eventual spontaneous immune clearance.
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical examination (dermoscopy of verruca shows pinpoint thrombosed black capillaries).
doctor_answer.management: Warts: Topical Salicylic Acid (17-40% with occlusion) or Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen Q2-3W). Plantar warts: pairing followed by cryotherapy. Molluscum: Watchful waiting (typically clears spontaneously in 6-18 months), topical cantharidin, or gentle curettage.
references: British Association of Dermatologists Guidelines for the Management of Cutaneous Warts
CDC Molluscum Contagiosum Guidance

staff_answer: Verify diagnosis. Confirm patient does not pick at lesions.
red_flags: Genital warts (Condyloma acuminata - requires evaluation for sexually transmitted HPV)
Rapidly proliferating extensive warts in immunocompromised patients
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT cut or slice warts off at home with razors or nail clippers (causes severe infection and scarring)
Do NOT share personal towels or pumice stones
source: British Association of Dermatologists & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Red Eye: Viral vs Bacterial vs Allergic Conjunctivitis
patient_answer: Red eye is most commonly caused by conjunctivitis (inflammation of the clear membrane covering the white of your eye).
DIFFERENTIATING TYPES OF CONJUNCTIVITIS:
- Viral ('Pink Eye'): Watery discharge, gritty feeling, starts in one eye and spreads to the other within 24 to 48 hours; highly contagious; resolves on its own in 1 to 2 weeks.
- Bacterial: Thick, yellow or green pus-like discharge that glues your eyelids shut in the morning; requires antibiotic eye drops.
- Allergic: Intense bilateral itching, watery eyes, and puffy swollen lids, often accompanied by sneezing and runny nose.
Clean discharge gently with clean cotton pads soaked in cooled boiled water, wiping from the inner corner outwards.
Do NOT wear contact lenses or eye makeup until the red eye has completely resolved.
DANGER SIGNS: If you have severe deep eye pain, sensitivity to light, or decreased vision, see an eye specialist immediately.

doctor_answer.assessment: Acute Conjunctivitis. Differentiate Viral vs Bacterial vs Allergic vs sight-threatening conditions (Keratitis, Acute Anterior Uveitis, Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma).
doctor_answer.investigations: Visual acuity testing (Snellen), slit-lamp biomicroscopy, fluorescein staining to rule out corneal abrasions/herpetic dendritic ulcers.
doctor_answer.management: Viral: Supportive (cold compresses, preservative-free artificial tears). Bacterial: Topical antibiotic drops (Moxifloxacin 0.5% or Tobramycin 0.3% QID for 5-7 days). Allergic: Topical Olopatadine 0.1% BID or Ketotifen drops.
references: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern: Conjunctivitis
RCOphth Clinical Guidelines on Management of Acute Red Eye

staff_answer: Check visual acuity and pupil reactivity. Ask if patient wears contact lenses (high risk for Pseudomonas keratitis).
red_flags: Severe deep eye pain or intense sensitivity to light (Photophobia)
Noticeable reduction in vision or cloudy cornea
Contact lens wearer with red eye and white corneal spot (Corneal Ulcer Emergency)
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: NEVER use steroid eye drops without an eye doctor's explicit examination (can cause corneal perforation or blindness if viral)
Do NOT share towels or eye drops
source: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) & Royal College of Ophthalmologists

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Dry Eye Disease & Digital Eye Strain (Computer Vision Syndrome)
patient_answer: Staring at smartphone, laptop, or TV screens reduces your natural blinking rate by over 60%, causing the protective tear film on your eyes to evaporate rapidly.
Symptoms: Gritty sensation (feeling like sand in the eyes), burning, redness, eye fatigue, and paradoxical watery tearing (reflex tears triggered by dry spots).
THE 20-20-20 RULE: Every 20 minutes of screen time, look at an object at least 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds to relax your eye focusing muscles.
Blink consciously: Make a deliberate effort to perform full, complete blinks while reading or working on screens.
Use preservative-free lubricating artificial tear drops 3 to 4 times a day to replenish moisture.
Screen setup: Position your monitor about arm's length away, with the top of the screen slightly below eye level so you look slightly downward (which exposes less eye surface to air).

doctor_answer.assessment: Dry Eye Disease (DED: Evaporative [Meibomian Gland Dysfunction] vs Aqueous Deficient) and Digital Eye Strain.
doctor_answer.investigations: Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT < 10s abnormal), Schirmer's test, ocular surface fluorescein staining, Meibography.
doctor_answer.management: Environmental and behavioral modification (20-20-20 rule, conscious blinking, humidification). Preservative-free artificial tears (Carboxymethylcellulose 0.5% or Sodium Hyaluronate 0.1-0.18%). Warm compresses and eyelid hygiene for Meibomian Gland Dysfunction. Topical Cyclosporine 0.05% or Lifitegrast for chronic inflammatory DED.
references: TFOS DEWS II (Tear Film & Ocular Surface Society Dry Eye Workshop II) Report
AAO Preferred Practice Pattern: Dry Eye Syndrome

staff_answer: Review daily screen hours and contact lens use. Demonstrate warm compress and lid massage technique.
red_flags: Severe persistent eye pain or foreign body sensation that does not improve with lubricating drops
Corneal abrasions or vision loss
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT use 'redness-reliever' eye drops (like naphazoline/decongestant drops) daily (causes severe rebound red eye)
Do NOT direct air conditioning fans or blowers straight at your face
source: TFOS DEWS II Global Consensus & American Academy of Ophthalmology

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Stye (Hordeolum) vs Chalazion (Eyelid Lumps)
patient_answer: A Stye (Hordeolum) is an acute, painful, red bacterial infection of an eyelash oil gland at the eyelid edge, looking like a tender red pimple.
A Chalazion is a painless, firm, non-infected lump deeper inside the eyelid caused by a blocked meibomian oil gland.
THE BEST TREATMENT: Warm compresses applied 3 to 4 times daily for 10 to 15 minutes each time. Soak a clean washcloth in warm water and place it gently over the closed eyelid.
The moist heat melts hardened oils inside the blocked gland, allowing it to drain and heal naturally.
NEVER POP OR SQUEEZE an eyelid bump; the eyelid tissues are delicate and popping can spread severe bacterial infection into the eye socket.
Do not wear eye makeup or contact lenses until the stye has completely drained and healed.
Consult an ophthalmologist if the bump does not shrink after 2 weeks, or if swelling spreads to the entire eyelid.

doctor_answer.assessment: Hordeolum (acute focal infection, internal [Meibomian] or external [Zeis/Moll], most commonly Staphylococcus aureus) vs Chalazion (chronic sterile lipogranulomatous inflammatory lesion of Meibomian gland).
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical slit-lamp examination. Evert eyelid to inspect tarsal conjunctiva.
doctor_answer.management: Frequent warm moist compresses (10-15 min TID-QID) + gentle eyelid margin hygiene. Topical antibiotic ointment (Erythromycin or Bacitracin) for external hordeolum. Persistent chalazion (>4-6 weeks): Incision and curettage under local anesthesia or intralesional triamcinolone injection.
references: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern: Blepharitis and Hordeolum
RCOphth Clinical Guidelines on Chalazion Management

staff_answer: Examine eyelid margin. Verify redness is localized to the lid and not spreading to the periorbital tissue.
red_flags: Swelling, redness, and heat spreading to the entire cheek or eyebrow with fever (Periorbital / Orbital Cellulitis - STAT Emergency)
Proptosis (eyeball protruding forward) or painful eye movement
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: NEVER squeeze, prick, or pop a stye with a pin (can cause orbital cellulitis or cavernous sinus thrombosis)
Do NOT apply warm compresses that are scalding hot
source: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) & Royal College of Ophthalmologists

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Glaucoma Warning Signs & Vision Preservation
patient_answer: Glaucoma ('Kala Motia') is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve, typically associated with elevated pressure inside the eye (Intraocular Pressure).

THE SILENT THIEF OF SIGHT: Open-Angle Glaucoma (the most common type) has ZERO pain and ZERO warning symptoms in early stages; it slowly steals peripheral (side) vision so gradually that patients do not notice until permanent tunnel vision occurs.
Vision lost to glaucoma can NEVER be recovered; however, early treatment with daily pressure-lowering eye drops completely halts further damage.
ACUTE ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA (SIGHT-THREATENING EMERGENCY):
- Sudden, severe, excruciating eye pain and headache.
- Rainbow-colored halos around bright lights.
- Severe nausea and vomiting.
- Red eye with a cloudy or steamy cornea and fixed, enlarged pupil.
If you experience sudden severe eye pain with halos, go to an eye hospital emergency department IMMEDIATELY.
Everyone aged 40 and older, and anyone with a family history of glaucoma, should have their eye pressure tested annually.

doctor_answer.assessment: Glaucoma: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG: chronic progressive optic neuropathy with cupping and visual field loss) vs Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG: acute or chronic appositional/synechial closure of anterior chamber angle).
doctor_answer.investigations: Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (IOP > 21 mmHg is elevated), Gonioscopy (angle assessment), Automated Visual Field perimetry (Humphrey visual fields: arcuate scotomas), Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT of retinal nerve fiber layer / RNFL).
doctor_answer.management: POAG: First-line Topical Prostaglandin Analogues (Latanoprost, Bimatoprost once daily bedtime). Second-line: Beta-blockers (Timolol 0.5%), Alpha-2 agonists, or Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT). Acute Angle-Closure Emergency: STAT medical pressure reduction (IV Mannitol, oral Acetazolamide 500 mg, topical Timolol, Pilocarpine 2%) followed by definitive bilateral Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI).
references: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma
EGS (European Glaucoma Society) Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Red for acute painful red eye with nausea and halos. Measure intraocular pressure immediately.
red_flags: Acute severe eye pain with blurred vision, halos around lights, and nausea/vomiting (Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma - STAT Emergency)
Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT skip daily prescribed glaucoma eye drops (IOP spikes silently when doses are missed)
Do NOT take over-the-counter anticholinergic or cold medications if diagnosed with narrow angles
source: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) & European Glaucoma Society (EGS)

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Sinusitis & Facial Pressure (Sinus Infection)
patient_answer: Sinusitis is inflammation of the air cavities inside your skull around your nose, forehead, and cheeks, most commonly following a viral cold.
Key signs: Facial pain, aching pressure behind the eyes, forehead, or cheekbones that worsens when bending forward, nasal congestion, and thick yellow or green nasal mucus.
Over 90% of acute sinus infections are VIRAL and resolve on their own within 7 to 10 days WITHOUT antibiotics.
Effective home relief:
- Inhale steam from a bowl of hot water or take a warm steamy shower for 10 minutes 2 to 3 times a day.
- Flush your sinuses with a saline nasal spray or sinus rinse bottle (use sterile/distilled water).
- Place a warm washcloth across your cheeks and forehead to ease pressure.
- Take Paracetamol or Ibuprofen for facial pain.
Consult a doctor if symptoms last more than 10 days without improvement, or if fever spikes after initially improving ('double sickening').

doctor_answer.assessment: Acute Rhinosinusitis (ARS: symptoms < 4 weeks). Differentiate Acute Viral Rhinosinusitis (AVRS) from Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis (ABRS: criteria = symptoms >= 10 days without improvement, severe onset [temp >=39°C + purulent rhinorrhea >=3-4 consecutive days], or 'double sickening' worsening).
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. Routine sinus CT is NOT recommended for uncomplicated ARS. CT Paranasal Sinuses indicated if orbital/intracranial complications or recurrent refractory disease.
doctor_answer.management: Symptomatic therapy for viral ARS: Saline nasal irrigation, Intranasal Corticosteroids (Mometasone / Fluticasone spray 2 sprays per nostril BID), analgesia. First-line for confirmed ABRS: Oral Amoxicillin-Clavulanate 875/125 mg BID for 5-7 days. Alternative in penicillin allergy: Doxycycline 100 mg BID.
references: IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis in Children and Adults
AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline: Adult Sinusitis

staff_answer: Check for orbital swelling, diplopia, or meningismus. Assess duration (>=10 days for bacterial suspicion).
red_flags: Swelling, redness, or pain around one eye socket (Periorbital / Orbital Cellulitis complication)
Severe unrelenting forehead headache with high fever and neck stiffness (Intracranial abscess / Meningitis)
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT use OTC nasal decongestant sprays (like Otrivin/Xylometazoline) for more than 3 to 5 days (causes severe rebound congestion)
Do NOT demand antibiotics for early sinus colds (<10 days)
source: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) & AAO-HNS Guidelines

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Earwax Impaction & Safe Ear Cleaning
patient_answer: Earwax (cerumen) is natural and healthy: it traps dirt, lubricates the ear canal, and contains enzymes that fight bacterial and fungal infections.
Your ears are naturally self-cleaning: chewing and jaw movements continuously migrate old earwax outwards to the ear opening where it flakes off.
Impaction occurs when wax builds up and blocks the canal, causing muffled hearing, fullness, ringing (tinnitus), or mild ear discomfort.

SAFE HOME SOFTENING: Instill 2 to 3 drops of plain mineral oil, baby oil, or earwax drops (such as carbamide peroxide or sodium bicarbonate drops) twice daily for 3 to 5 days to soften the wax so it drains naturally.

STRICT GOLDEN RULE: NEVER insert cotton swabs (Q-tips), safety pins, matchsticks, or car keys into your ear canal; swabs act like a piston that pushes wax deeper, packing it against your delicate eardrum and risking eardrum puncture.
If hearing remains blocked, visit an ENT clinic for painless ear syringing or micro-suction removal under direct vision.

doctor_answer.assessment: Cerumen Impaction (accumulation of cerumen causing symptoms [hearing loss, otalgia, tinnitus, fullness] or preventing necessary clinical examination).
doctor_answer.investigations: Otoscopic examination (identifies dark yellow, brown, or black cerumen completely occluding external auditory canal).
doctor_answer.management: Options: 1. Cerumenolytic drops (Carbamide peroxide 6.5%, mineral oil, sodium bicarbonate 5% drops for 3-5 days). 2. Irrigation with body-temperature water (must confirm tympanic membrane is intact without perforation). 3. Manual removal / Micro-suction under direct microscopic or otoscopic visualization by trained clinician.
references: AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline: Cerumen Impaction (Update)
NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: Earwax

staff_answer: Examine canal with otoscope. Verify water temperature is strictly body temperature (37°C) before irrigation (cold/hot water triggers violent caloric vertigo).
red_flags: Sudden sharp excruciating pain with hearing loss and bleeding while inserting a swab (Traumatic Tympanic Membrane Perforation)
Severe pain and foul drainage in an elderly diabetic patient (Malignant Otitis Externa)
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: NEVER insert cotton buds, keys, or foreign objects into your ear canal
Do NOT use 'Ear Candling' (completely ineffective and causes severe ear burns and canal obstruction)
source: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS)

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Gingivitis & Bleeding Gums (Gum Health Basics)
patient_answer: Gingivitis is the early, reversible stage of gum disease caused by dental plaque (a sticky film of bacteria) accumulating along the gumline.
Key signs: Gums that bleed easily when you brush or floss, red swollen tender gums, and persistent bad breath (halitosis).
If neglected, gingivitis advances to Periodontitis: the gum tissue pulls away from the teeth, bone support dissolves, and teeth become loose and fall out.
Daily oral hygiene essentials:
- Brush your teeth thoroughly twice a day for a full 2 minutes using a soft-bristled toothbrush and fluoride toothpaste.
- Floss between your teeth once a day to clean food and plaque from tight spaces your toothbrush bristles cannot reach.
- Rinse with a warm salt water rinse or antiseptic mouthwash.
Do NOT stop brushing or flossing because your gums bleed; gentle, thorough cleaning removes the bacterial plaque that causes the bleeding in the first place.
Visit a dentist every 6 months for professional scaling and cleaning to remove hardened tartar (calculus).

doctor_answer.assessment: Gingivitis (plaque-induced gingival inflammation without loss of attachment) vs Periodontitis (irreversible destruction of periodontal ligament and alveolar bone). Screen for systemic associations (diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, smoking, leukemia).
doctor_answer.investigations: Periodontal probing depth measurements (probing depths > 3 mm indicate periodontal pocketing). Full mouth dental radiographs (OPG / periapical).
doctor_answer.management: Professional dental scaling and root planing (deep cleaning). Oral hygiene instruction: Bass brushing technique, daily interdental flossing. Chlorhexidine gluconate 0.12% mouthwash short-term (max 2 weeks to prevent tooth staining). Treat systemic comorbidities (glycemic control in diabetics).
references: AAP / EFP World Workshop on the Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases
ADA Guidelines on Periodontal Disease

staff_answer: Inquire about brushing frequency, flossing, and history of diabetes or blood thinners.
red_flags: Rapid spontaneous gum bleeding accompanied by easy skin bruising, extreme fatigue, and fever (screen for Acute Leukemia)
Teeth becoming visibly loose and shifting position
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT stop brushing because your gums bleed (cleaning clears the bacterial cause of bleeding)
Do NOT use stiff hard-bristled toothbrushes (damages enamel and recedes gums)
source: American Dental Association (ADA) & European Federation of Periodontology

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Dental Abscess & Severe Tooth Infection
patient_answer: A dental abscess is a localized collection of pus caused by a severe bacterial infection that spreads from an untreated dental cavity into the root of the tooth or surrounding jawbone.

Key signs: Severe, continuous, throbbing tooth pain that radiates to your jaw, ear, or neck, extreme sensitivity to hot and cold, swelling in your cheek or jaw, and a foul taste in your mouth if the abscess ruptures.
First aid while waiting for dental care:
- Take Ibuprofen (400 mg with food) or Paracetamol for pain and inflammation.
- Rinse gently with warm salt water (1/2 teaspoon salt in a glass of warm water) 3 to 4 times a day.
- Hold an ice pack wrapped in a cloth against the outside of your cheek for 15 minutes.
URGENT DENTAL ATTENTION IS MANDATORY: An abscess will NEVER heal on its own; a dentist must drain the infection and perform root canal treatment or extract the tooth.

AIRWAY EMERGENCY WARNING: If swelling spreads down into your neck, under your tongue, or makes it difficult to swallow or breathe, go to a hospital emergency room IMMEDIATELY (concern for Ludwig's Angina).

doctor_answer.assessment: Periapical Abscess vs Periodontal Abscess. High risk of fascial space infection (Ludwig's Angina / Submandibular space cellulitis) and cavernous sinus thrombosis.
doctor_answer.investigations: Dental periapical radiograph, panoramic OPG. Check for trismus (inability to open mouth) and floor-of-mouth elevation.
doctor_answer.management: Urgent dental referral for drainage: incision and drainage or pulpectomy/root canal therapy. Analgesia: NSAIDs + Paracetamol. Systemic antibiotics indicated if systemic signs (fever, lymphadenopathy, cellulitis): Amoxicillin-Clavulanate 625 mg TID or Clindamycin 300 mg QID for 5-7 days.
references: ADA Clinical Practice Guideline on Antibiotic Use for Odontogenic Infections
NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: Dental Abscess

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Red if facial/neck swelling with difficulty swallowing or breathing. Check for floor-of-mouth elevation and trismus.
red_flags: Swelling spreading into the neck or floor of the mouth, causing difficulty swallowing or breathing (Ludwig's Angina - Critical Airway Emergency)
Inability to open mouth wider than 1 finger (Severe Trismus)
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: NEVER place an Aspirin tablet directly against your gum or tooth (causes severe chemical burn and tissue necrosis)
Do NOT delay dental treatment hoping antibiotics alone will cure an abscess
source: American Dental Association (ADA) & American Association of Endodontists

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Mouth Ulcers & Canker Sores (Aphthous Stomatitis)
patient_answer: Canker sores (Aphthous ulcers) are small, painful, shallow oval ulcers with a white or yellowish center and a bright red border appearing inside the cheeks, lips, gums, or under the tongue.
They are NOT contagious and are NOT caused by cold sores (herpes virus).
Common triggers: Accidental cheek biting, sharp food scratches, stress, lack of sleep, Vitamin B12 / iron deficiency, or food sensitivities (acidic fruits, spicy chili).
Soothing relief:
- Rinse with warm salt water (1/2 teaspoon salt in 1 cup warm water) 3 times daily.
- Apply an over-the-counter soothing oral gel containing Choline Salicylate, Benzocaine, or protective hyaluronic acid over the ulcer before meals.
- Avoid spicy, salty, citrus, and rough crunchy foods that cause sharp burning pain.
Most canker sores heal completely on their own within 7 to 10 days.
RED FLAG: ANY mouth ulcer that lasts longer than 3 WEEKS without healing MUST be examined by a dentist or ENT specialist to rule out oral cancer.

doctor_answer.assessment: Recurrent Aphthous Stomatitis (RAS: Minor <10 mm, Major >10 mm, Herpetiform). Differentiate from Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OSCC), Behcet's disease, Crohn's disease, and Celiac disease.
doctor_answer.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. Laboratory workup for recurrent ulcers: CBC, Serum Ferritin, Vitamin B12, Folate, anti-tTG IgA. Incisional biopsy mandatory for any non-healing indurated ulcer persisting > 3 weeks.
doctor_answer.management: Topical analgesia/anesthetic gels (Benzocaine/Lidocaine gel). Topical anti-inflammatory: Triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% dental paste applied QID after meals. Antimicrobial mouth rinse (Chlorhexidine 0.2%). Supplement nutritional deficiencies.
references: AAO-HNS Clinical Guidelines on Aphthous Ulcers
British Dental Association Clinical Reference

staff_answer: Inquire about ulcer duration. Inspect ulcer base (firm induration requires biopsy). Screen for tobacco/areca nut use.
red_flags: Mouth ulcer persisting for longer than 3 WEEKS without healing (Mandatory Oral Biopsy to rule out Oral Cancer)
Ulcer accompanied by hard, enlarged, non-tender neck lymph nodes
Multiple deep painful ulcers accompanied by genital ulcers and eye inflammation (Behcet's Disease)
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT ignore a painless or painful mouth ulcer that lasts longer than 3 weeks
Do NOT use tobacco, gutkha, paan, or supari (primary causes of oral pre-cancer and cancer)
source: American Academy of Oral Medicine & British Dental Association

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Nosebleeds First Aid & Epistaxis Management
patient_answer: CORRECT FIRST AID TO STOP A NOSEBLEED:
1. Sit upright and LEAN SLIGHTLY FORWARD. (Do NOT tilt your head backwards; tilting backwards causes blood to drain down into your throat and stomach, triggering vomiting and choking).
2. PINCH THE SOFT LOWER PART OF YOUR NOSE (just below the bony bridge) firmly using your thumb and index finger.
3. Hold continuous, uninterrupted pressure for AT LEAST 10 TO 15 FULL MINUTES while breathing calmly through your mouth.
4. Apply an ice pack or cold damp cloth across the bridge of your nose and forehead to constrict blood vessels.
5. After 15 minutes, gently release pressure. Do NOT blow your nose, pick inside, or bend over for several hours to keep the blood clot intact.

SEEK EMERGENCY CARE IF: Bleeding does not stop after 20 minutes of firm direct pressure, bleeding is heavy and flowing down the back of your throat, or if the nosebleed started after a severe head blow.

doctor_answer.assessment: Epistaxis: Anterior (Kiesselbach's / Little's plexus on anterior septum ~90%) vs Posterior (Sphenopalatine artery ~10%, common in elderly/hypertensive, high airway compromise risk).
doctor_answer.investigations: Check vital signs (blood pressure), CBC, PT/INR, aPTT if on anticoagulants or frequent recurrent bleeds.
doctor_answer.management: Firm continuous compression of anterior nasal cartilages for 15 minutes with forward lean. Topical vasoconstrictor (Oxymetazoline or Phenylephrine spray). Chemical cautery with Silver Nitrate (75%) if discrete bleeding vessel visualized on anterior septum. Anterior nasal packing (Rapid Rhino or Merocel) if compression fails. Posterior packing / balloon catheter and hospital admission for posterior bleeds.
references: AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline: Nosebleed (Epistaxis)
NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: Epistaxis

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Yellow/Red based on blood loss and hemodynamic stability. Check BP immediately. Ensure patient leans FORWARD.
red_flags: Bleeding continuing unabated after 20 minutes of continuous direct pressure
Posterior bleeding with large volumes of blood pouring down the pharynx
Nosebleed accompanied by dizziness, pallor, or SBP < 90 mmHg (Hemorrhagic shock)
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: NEVER tilt your head backwards during a nosebleed (causes blood swallowing, vomiting, and airway aspiration)
Do NOT pack your nose with dry tissue paper or unsterile cotton
source: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS)

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Foreign Body in Eye, Ear, or Nose First Aid
patient_answer: FOREIGN OBJECT IN THE EYE (Dust, eyelash, insect):
- Blink repeatedly in a cup of clean, lukewarm water or flush gently with saline eye drops.
- Pull the upper eyelid gently down over the lower lid so lower lashes sweep out the particle.
- NEVER RUB YOUR EYE; rubbing scratches the clear cornea with the sharp particle (corneal abrasion).
- If a metal fragment, chemical, or sharp object penetrates the eye: do NOT touch it, tape a protective paper cup over the eye, and go to an eye hospital IMMEDIATELY.
CHILD WITH OBJECT IN NOSE (Bead, button battery, pea):
- Practice the 'Mother's Kiss': cover the clear nostril with a finger, place your mouth over the child's mouth, and deliver a quick puff of air to pop the object out.
- NEVER use tweezers to blindly poke inside the nose (pushes the object deeper into the breathing airway).

DANGER: BUTTON BATTERIES: If a tiny circular button battery is stuck in the ear or nose, it releases electric current and caustic alkali that destroys tissue within 2 hours; seek EMERGENCY hospital removal immediately.

doctor_answer.assessment: Foreign body in sensory organ (Corneal/conjunctival foreign body, Aural foreign body, Nasal foreign body). High-risk categories: Button batteries (rapid tissue necrosis), magnetic objects, penetrating intraocular foreign bodies.
doctor_answer.investigations: Eye: Slit-lamp exam, fluorescein stain with cobalt blue light (demonstrates corneal epithelial defect / Seidel's test for perforation). ENT: Otoscopy, anterior rhinoscopy.
doctor_answer.management: Superficial ocular FB: Gentle saline irrigation or moist cotton swab under topical anesthesia. Button battery in ear/nose: IMMEDIATE STAT emergency endoscopic extraction. Live insect in ear: Instill mineral oil to suffocate insect before gentle removal.
references: AAO Preferred Practice Patterns: Eye Trauma
AAO-HNS Clinical Guidance on Pediatric Foreign Bodies

staff_answer: Priority: Triage Red if button battery lodged in nose/ear or penetrating eye injury. Keep patient NPO for potential ENT removal under anesthesia.
red_flags: Button battery lodged in nose or ear (Emergency tissue liquefactive necrosis within 2 hours)
Penetrating eye injury with distorted pupil or leaking fluid (STAT Ophthalmology)
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT blindly dig inside the ear or nose with tweezers or pins (risks pushing object into lungs or puncturing eardrum)
Do NOT rub an eye containing a foreign object
source: American Academy of Ophthalmology & AAO-HNS Clinical Guidance

topic: Skin, Eye, ENT & Dental: Cataracts (Safed Motia) & Modern Phaco Surgery
patient_answer: A Cataract is a natural clouding of the clear lens inside your eye, occurring predominantly as a normal part of aging (usually starting after age 55 to 60).

Key signs: Gradual, painless blurring of vision (feeling like looking through a foggy or frosted glass window), colors appearing faded or yellowed, difficulty driving at night due to glare from oncoming headlights, and needing brighter light to read.
Eye drops, exercises, diets, or glasses CANNOT dissolve or cure a cataract; surgery is the only scientifically proven treatment.

When is surgery needed? Cataract surgery is NOT an emergency; you can choose surgery whenever cloudy vision begins to interfere with your daily activities (reading, watching TV, cooking, or driving safely).

Modern Phacoemulsification surgery: A quick, painless, 15-minute outpatient procedure performed under numbing eye drops (no needle injection); an ultrasound probe liquefies the cloudy lens, and a clear foldable Intraocular Lens (IOL) is inserted.

doctor_answer.assessment: Age-Related Cataract (Nuclear Sclerosis, Cortical, Posterior Subcapsular). Differentiate from Glaucoma, Macular Degeneration, and Diabetic Retinopathy.
doctor_answer.investigations: Visual acuity, Slit-lamp biomicroscopy after pupillary dilation, Intraocular lens (IOL) power calculation via Optical Biometry (IOLMaster / Lenstar). Dilated fundus examination.
doctor_answer.management: Definitive curative management: Micro-Incision Cataract Surgery (MICS / Phacoemulsification) with foldable IOL implantation (Monofocal, Toric for astigmatism, or Multifocal/EDOF for spectacle independence) under topical anesthesia. Postoperative care: Topical antibiotic-corticosteroid drops tapered over 4 weeks.
references: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern: Cataract in the Adult Eye
RCOphth Cataract Surgery Guidelines

staff_answer: Verify patient understands surgery is elective based on functional visual goals. Review systemic medications (Alpha-blockers like Tamsulosin cause Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome / IFIS).
red_flags: Severe acute eye pain, redness, and rapid vision loss days after cataract surgery (Acute Postoperative Endophthalmitis - STAT Emergency)
Dense hypermature morgagnian cataract causing phacolytic glaucoma
follow_up_questions: How long have you had this symptom?
Is there any severe pain, discharge, or changes in vision or hearing?
Have you applied any creams or drops already?
avoid: Do NOT purchase unproven OTC eye drops claiming to 'dissolve cataracts'
Do NOT rub your eye or splash tap water into the eye during the first 2 weeks after surgery
source: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) & Royal College of Ophthalmologists
